title: Lego marketplace BrickLink offline after 'unusual activity' detected
content: Lego has taken its online marketplace BrickLink offline after detecting what it described as unusual activity on the platform. BrickLink is used by Lego collectors worldwide to buy and sell secondhand Lego sets, source new bricks and purchase limited edition releases. It was originally set up by a fan, but Lego acquired it in 2019. In a homepage message, the firm said that before restoring BrickLink, it wanted to "fully understand" what had happened. "That means containing the issue, investigating how it happened and checking for related issues," Lego said. It did not provide any further detail about whether the site has been breached or hacked, and whether any customer data was affected. After being contacted by the BBC, Lego published the update. BrickLink has been offline for the last three days, with a previous message saying it was down for maintenance. Cyber-professional Melanie Hoskin has been collecting Lego for 45 years and is a regular user of BrickLink. She told the BBC she had received multiple links for payment for a limited edition release she had pre-ordered on the platform, after she had already paid for it. She said Lego did not believe that the payment had been taken and at one point said it would ban her from BrickLink. The problem has now been resolved and Lego said it was not aware of wider payment issues. It is unclear if the payment glitch had any connection to the issue that led to the website going offline. Hoskin said she felt like she had been accused of theft. "Lego is my stress relief," she said. "Lego is what I grew up with as a kid, it's what bonded me with my sisters. "I've got a Lego room and I've not even been able to walk into it this past couple of weeks because it just angers me." Earlier today, a message on BrickLink said the platform would be back online by Wednesday evening, but that message has now been deleted and there is no longer a time frame given for its return.

title: Judge allows Trump's $10bn defamation case against BBC to proceed
content: A federal judge in Florida has allowed US President Donald Trump's defamation case against the BBC to go ahead after the broadcaster sought to dismiss it. But Judge Jeffrey Kuntz dismissed a second claim in the $10bn (£7.5bn) lawsuit under the state's unfair trade practices law. The US president is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the riot at the US Capitol in 2021. Trump called the judge's ruling a "huge victory" in a Truth Social post on Tuesday. A BBC spokesperson said: "We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court's authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage." The BBC spokesperson added: "We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process." Judge Kuntz found Trump's defamation allegations against the BBC sufficient for the case to continue, although he did not make a ruling on the merits of the case. "Whether President Trump can prove these claims and establish he sustained damages at summary judgment or trial is left for another day," he wrote in Tuesday's order. Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021. The BBC apologised and said that the broadcast had given "the mistaken impression that Trump made a direct call for violent action". The broadcaster has since asked that the court dismiss the lawsuit, arguing the programme does not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not available in the US. Along with defamation, Trump claimed in the lawsuit that the broadcaster had violated Florida law, specifically the Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. Kuntz on Tuesday dismissed that part of the lawsuit, ruling that the documentary did not constitute commercial speech. A judge ordered Trump last month to answer questions under oath in the lawsuit by 11 December, after the president cancelled a previous deposition last month, citing "matters of national importance". A lawyer representing the BBC said in court that Trump was campaigning in Georgia in October on the scheduled day and had "prioritised that" over answering their questions. Earlier this year, Trump's lawyers conceded they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC's BritBox subscription service - as they originally argued - or on the BBC's website, BBC Select or through US broadcasters. Trump ultimately agreed to drop BBC Studios, the broadcaster's commercial arm, from his defamation lawsuit, after the BBC argued that it had "no role in creating or producing the documentary". title: From Paris to DC - why offices are being turned into apartments
content: When Roland Cubin walks you round what will eventually be a new Parisian apartment you have to use your imagination. "Here you will be in the kitchen, and here is the bathroom," says the deputy CEO of French real estate company Groupama Immobilier. It all sounds appealing, an upmarket flat in the west of Paris, but presently the space doesn't look like one at all. That's because it's currently a corner of one floor of a nine-storey office building called Le Diamant, where 1,800 people work. Groupama Immobilier intends to convert the entire building into apartments. It should be the first of many such office-to-apartments conversions in the surrounding area. We are in La Défense, the purpose-built, business district of the French capital, where the city has congregated its modern skyscrapers. Mirroring a similar trend in places such as New York, Washington DC and London; Paris La Défense, the public development authority that runs the area, has unveiled plans to turn up to a fifth of the office buildings into housing. Cubin leads us into what is currently a conference room in the centre of the building. It has no windows, which is indicative of a big challenge when turning offices into apartments – what to do with the large amount of space in the middle of every floor that doesn't get any natural light. "There won't be any rooms there. Just access," says Roland Cubin, in reference to lifts and stairs. Other issues include the need for more plumbing, and ceilings that can be too low. Despite these challenges, there is a simple reason why there are plans for so many conversions – demand for offices in La Défense and across Paris has plummeted since the Covid-19 pandemic and the growth of homeworking. "La Défense has a vacancy rate of 14-15% which is higher than it used to be," says Pierre-Yves Guice, CEO of Paris La Défense. He adds that another reason for the conversion programme is the need to transform the business district from a place where the only thing people do is work. "To retain companies in France and in Western Europe we need to diversify these office landscapes of the last century, because no-one wants to work in such an environment any longer," says Guice. Ludovic Delaisse, CEO of the French arm of the Canadian real estate business Colliers, says that demand for office space in Paris has fallen by almost a third over the past five to six years. He adds that office high rises will continue to be needed, but that cities need to make sure that leisure time can be enjoyed around them, such as having restaurants, bars, cinemas and gyms on their doorstep. "People like the idea of grouping together in a centre of expertise [for work] - in tech hubs, for example. The challenge for La Défense is to be a place where you want to be, that you want to see when you leave work in the evening." Inspiration for La Défense can come from Washington DC and New York City, where tax cuts for property developers are fuelling the largest amount of office to apartment conversions in the US. Like in Paris, this is in response to falling demand for office space since the pandemic. A report last year found that 8,310 converted flats were in the pipeline in New York, and 6,533 in Washington. In third place was Los Angeles on 4,322, followed by Chicago on 3,606. "We set a goal of introducing 15,000 new residents downtown by 2028 and we are now on track to doing that," says Washington DC's deputy mayor for planning and development Nina Albert. She says that while "there may be one or two pretty significant building demolitions… the majority are office conversions". As in Paris, they've faced technical challenges. They've sometimes solved the natural light problem in the middle of office buildings by creating atriums – light sinks in other words – in the middle of them. Albert adds that about "hundreds of millions of dollars of private investment" has flooded into the sector. In addition to tax cuts, the DC Department of Buildings, part of the Council of the District of Columbia, has eased planning restrictions to make it easier for office conversion schemes to gain official approval in the US capital. It's a similar case in New York City. In the UK, there are also tax cuts and eased planning rules for converting offices into apartments. This has led to a continuing boom in conversions. A report last year by property firm Knight Frank said that the number of such projects in London were 60% higher than pre-Covid levels. Back in Paris, Cubin hopes that French authorities follow these examples and reduce both taxes and rules regarding conversions. "Just how the government deals with the tax question will decide whether France will be able to convert 2% of its vacant offices or 18 to 23%," he says. "And at the moment, when you transform a building in a way that changes its function, it is classed not as an old building that's been changed but as a new building with all the regulatory demands that go with that regarding car parking spaces, wheelchair access, fire safety and so on."

title: A new fire-suppression system fights flames with sound waves
content: Forget water: An Ohio company has found a way to fight fires with sound waves. The technology could extinguish a blaze without drenching your home or business. Each year, there are around 330,000 home fires in the US, resulting in 2,600 civilian deaths. While the number of home fires has halved since 1980, fire fighters today are facing new challenges. Modern homes experience more grease-related fires, with more people cooking with oil than in the past. Lithium-ion batteries are becoming increasingly common — which the US Department of Commerce says have caused more than 200,000 fires since 2011 Now, Sonic Fire Tech has developed a technology it says can extinguish fires without drawing on strained municipal water supplies or causing water damage — using low-frequency sound waves. The company has developed an acoustic generator that can be housed inside a building, and produces high-pressure infrasound waves. These travel through a dedicated ducting system, much like plumbing or HVAC. Sonic Fire Tech says the sound waves vibrate oxygen molecules and push them away faster than the fuel can use them. Since fire needs oxygen to sustain itself, without it, the flames starve. “We want to fight fires without the inconveniences of conventional suppression,” co-founder and CEO of Sonic Fire Tech Geoff Bruder said. “A traditional sprinkler triggers when it senses heat between 135 and 165 degrees Fahrenheit, which takes at least three minutes of burning fire. And then, it unleashes 8 to 24 gallons of water per minute into the room it’s installed in.” Sonic Fire Tech’s system activates the moment it detects heat. Because sound waves cause no damage to the building, there’s no reason to wait; if it’s a false alarm, there’s no harm done. The sound waves are below the audible range of 20 Hz, so humans and pets can’t hear them. “What makes our system especially promising is that it can suppress grease fires — something water-based systems can’t do,” Bruder said. The estimated installation cost for a 3,500 square feet home is $30,000 or around $8.50 per square foot. The US Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) has previously studied the idea of using sound to suppress fires, and a decade ago students at George Mason University found a way to miniaturize the technology. But Bruder says his background helped take it to the next level. “I’m an aerospace engineer. I started my career at NASA, working on power systems for planetary missions,” he said. There, he converted “heat energy into acoustic waves, then into power and cooling for a lander designed to survive on Venus.” That expertise was what lawyer Michael Thomas, the company’s co-founder and board chairman, was looking for to develop the technology, which he had been studying “as a side-project” since the 2000s. In 2019, after connecting on LinkedIn, the two founded Sonic Fire Tech, working “nights and weekends” around their full-time jobs on an early prototype. In 2025, they raised $3.5 million in funding, before a $15 million round in August 2026, led by the O.H.I.O. Fund . Dr. Michael J. Gollner, an associate professor of mechanical engineering at the University of California, Berkeley, who is chair of the Research Advisory Board of the NFPA Fire Protection Research Foundation, is familiar with the concept of using sound waves to extinguish fires. In 2015, he judged a thesis by a Berkeley student working on a similar technology. He sees promise, with limits. “At small scales and directed very close, the technology works well,” Gollner explained. “But whether it’s as efficient on big flames and in the long term still has to be proven.” He added that, despite the damage they can cause to a building once activated, “water suppression sprinklers are terribly efficient, and this new technology still needs to prove that it’s more efficient than this.” Today, Sonic Fire Tech employs around 20 people and is working toward certification. Interior fire suppression is already mandated in hundreds of local jurisdictions in the US, which gives the company a defined path to approval: in the short term, the Authority Having Jurisdiction — for example fire marshals — can approve individual installations. Sonic Fire Tech holds three permits in LA County and has begun its first installation in Altadena. This comes in the wake of the deadly Eaton Fire in 2025, which exposed infrastructure gaps where water shortages and dry hydrants hindered emergency response teams. The company has signed two reseller agreements with California home builders. In the longer term, a national lab must test and certify the system before it can be an option that architects and home builders can use for new homes — and potentially for businesses and data centers too. Bruder said certification testing was expected to begin this autumn, and they expect the first fire and safety certification in 2027. Last year, the San Bernardino County Fire Protection District participated in demonstrations with Sonic Fire Tech to evaluate the technology, including in-house simulation and wearable acoustic suppression backpacks. “Our personnel got to observe the technology and its capabilities, including possible applications for use by firefighters,” said Ryan Beckers, the San Bernardino County Fire Protection District public information officer. “We found the technology intriguing, particularly as a potential alternative to water-based home and industrial business sprinkler systems.” Beyond interior suppression, Sonic Fire Tech wants to eventually use sound waves to fight wildfires. In recent years, the US, and particularly California, has experienced devastating fires that have become easier to ignite and harder to contain as the result of a worsening climate crisis. The company hopes to alleviate the strain on water supplies without contributing to the environmental pollution associated with chemical retardants, which are often laden with toxic metals . Sonic Fire Tech has started a research project with the Cal Poly Wildland-Urban Interface (WUI) Fire Institute, the first step toward the full-scale testing insurers have asked for. “The fire situation in California really put people’s minds onto fire as a problem,” Bruder said. “The state really turned their attention to us once they realized how big a problem fire was and that water was not always going to be available.”
